Effect on cell surface markers following allergen-induced desensitization of human whole-blood basophils; Background: Allergen-specific immunotherapy (SIT) leads to reduced symptoms upon allergen exposure through as yet unresolved mechanisms. Desensitization of basophils to specific allergens during the updosing phase of injection immunotherapy may contribute to the clinical effect of SIT. Here we report a protocol for efficient in vitro allergen-mediated desensitization of basophils in whole blood and the effect of desensitization on the expression of basophil activation markers (CD203c and CD63) as well as histamine release in response to allergen challenge. Methods: Whole blood from grass pollen-allergic subjects was incubated with Phleum pratense extract by stepwise increase of the allergen concentration in the culture from well below to well above the allergen threshold concentration for activation of basophils. Desensitization was determined by measuring the expression of the basophil activation markers CD63 and CD203c by FACS following challenge with high allergen concentrations. Results: The basophil desensitization protocol reported here affected both the expression of the cell-surface markers and the levels of histamine release. Following the stepwise desensitization procedure the whole-blood basophils were not activated when challenged with more than 10-fold increased allergen concentration. Conclusion: We have established a protocol for basophil desensitization. By mimicking the updosing phase of immunotherapy we raised the allergen threshold for basophil activation and obtained efficient desensitization for all donors. We showed that conditions leading to desensitization affect histamine release and expression of different basophil markers alike. Copyright © 2010 S. Karger AG, Basel.
Subcutaneous specific immunotherapy: The patients' perspective; Background: In allergic asthma and/or rhinitis, specific immunotherapy (SIT) may favourably change the course of the disease. Objectives: To assess, in a population of patients with respiratory allergy receiving subcutaneous SIT (SCIT), their perception regarding efficacy and safety of SCIT. Material and methods: Self-administered questionnaire applied in May/2010 to all adult patients with respiratory allergy, SCIT-treated for >1 year, that came to our hospital's Allergy Clinic to receive their monthly SCIT injection. Patients were asked about any adverse reactions and their timing of appearance, as well as any pain or apprehension associated with the allergen injection (visual analog pain scale). Patients were also asked about their perception of the efficacy of SCIT regarding symptoms and medication use and about their preference regarding SIT route (subcutaneous or sublingual). Results: The levels of pain and fear associated with SCIT injections are relatively low, as is the frequency of adverse reactions reported by patients. Systemic reactions are more frequently associated to pollen SCIT but recurrent reactions are more frequently seen in mite SCIT. Sublingual route is preferred by 42% of patients with frequent or very frequent adverse reactions. According to patients, most adverse reactions (54%) occur within the first 2 hours after SCIT injection. SCIT is associated with patients' perception of clinical improvement, as well as with reduction of need for pharmacological therapy, particularly in SCIT-treated patients for ≥3 years, in whom, the proportion of patients without any treatment in the previous 24 hours is significantly higher. Conclusion: In general, SCIT is seen as safe, effective and associated with clinical improvement, reduction of medication need and only a little discomfort. Most SCIT-treated patients find it easier to remember and prefer this to sublingual daily administrations.
Efficacy and safety of grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) in a North American pediatric population; Background: A number of immunological changes have been previously reported in subjects undergoing specific immunotherapy, particularly changes in allergen specific antibody responses. A phase 3, randomized trial was conducted to investigate the efficacy and tolerability of a new grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) and its effects on IgG4 levels and IgE blocking factor in North American children. Methods: IRB approval was obtained at all sites and written informed consent obtained from subjects/legal guardians. 345 children (5-17 yrs) with grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were randomized 1:1 to once-daily 2800 BAU grass AIT (oral lyophilisate, Phleum pratense) or placebo (PBO) beginning approximately 16 weeks before and continuing through the 2009 grass pollen season (GPS). The primary efficacy endpoint was the total combined daily symptom and medication score (TCS). Specific IgG4 levels and IgE-blocking factor were measured before, during, and at the end of GPS. Safety was assessed by adverse events (AEs). Results: The mean GPS lasted 43 days (mean grass pollen count 28 grains/m3). 89% of subjects were multisensitized. The effect of grassAIT on IgG4 levels was significantly greater compared with PBO at peak season (P<0.001) and increased through the end of GPS (P<0.001). Similarly, the effect of grass AIT on IgE blocking factor was significantly greater compared with PBO at peak season (P<0.001) and was sustained through the end of GPS. The majority of treatment-related AEs were local, application site reactions. Conclusions: We report the first successful phase III pediatric grass AIT trial in North America. Once-daily administration of grass AIT is effective and well-tolerated, representing a new therapeutic modality for children with grass pollen-induced allergy. The effect of treatment on the immune system was confirmed by the changes in immunologic parameters, specifically increases in specific IgG4 and IgE blocking factor.

Stability of allergen extracts diluted in saline or human serum albumin solutions; Introduction: Allergen extract concentrate vials are labeled with expiration dates, and when standardized the dating is verified by potency testing. Only a few studies have been performed to determine the stability of these extracts once they are diluted for use in immunotherapy (IT). Previous studies have shown that adding a protein carrier to the diluting solution may improve the stability, but these studies are limited due to the lack of sensitive analytical methods. This study investigates stability of dilute extracts using in vitro allergen potency methods. Methods: Standardized dust mite, Timothy grass, Cat Hair, and non-standardized Birch and English plantain extracts were tested for total protein by Brandford type Coomassie Plus assay. The extracts were diluted to 1 microgram per mL of protein. Dilutions were prepared using saline-phenol diluent (NSP) supplemented with human serum albumin (HSA) at concentrations ranging from 0 to 300μg/mL. The diluted extract solutions were stored at 2-8°C for 7 days and up to 3 months. Extracts were also diluted in NSP to 1 to 100 μg/mL total protein. Potency was measured using major allergen ELISAs developed by ALK-Abelló. IgE binding assays and SDS-PAGE were also used to assess stability. Results. The extracts were diluted in 5mL glass serum vials. Extract dilutions were between 1:100v/v and 1:2500v/v. Each allergen extract maintained expected major allergen content in 300 and 100 μg/mL HSA. However, after just 6 days each extract lost allergen protein in a dose dependent manner in 33, 11, 4, 1 and 0 μg/mL HSA. For example, English plantain lost 66% Pla l 1 in 11 μg/mL HSA. Similar protein-dependent loss of allergen was seen when the extracts were diluted 3 fold serially from 100 μg/mL to 1 μg/mL. Timothy grass Phl p 5 decreased 50% when diluted 1:200v/v. The loss of major allergens was confirmed with electrophoresis and IgE binding titration. Glycerin at 10% or 50% did not prevent the loss of allergens in the low protein solutions. Conclusions. Extracts diluted as typically done for IT lose allergen content when the protein level drops below about 4 to 30 μg/mL. Use of diluent containing HSA can prevent this loss of in vitro allergenic activity.

Assessment of sustained efficacy and safety of a 300IR 5-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy tablet (SLIT) in adults with grass pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis during a 3-year treatment study; Background: In single-season clinical trials, once-daily pre-coseasonal treatment with a 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet was shown to be safe and effective in adults and children. The aim of this study was to evaluate the sustained efficacy and safety of pre-coseasonal treatment with 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet in adults with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Methods: 633 patients aged between 18 and 51 years were included in a DBPC, international, multi-centre Phase III trial to evaluate the sustained efficacy and safety of the 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet over 3 consecutive seasons. Patients were randomized to a placebo and 2 active groups, receiving either 4 or 2 months of pre-seasonal treatment and co-seasonal treatment. Use of rescue medication was permitted. The primary efficacy endpoint was the Average Adjusted Symptom Score (AAdSS, a score that integrates the symptoms and rescue medication use) over the 3rd pollen season. Results: 457 patients completed 3 consecutive seasons (2007, 2008 and 2009). Preliminary results of the 3rd pollen period showed a meanAAdSS±SD of 3.51±3.68 and 3.39±3.23 for the 4 and 2 months pre-seasonal treatment groups respectively, compared with 5.28±3.95 in placebo group. The efficacy of 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet seems to increase at every season, reaching a meanAAdSS improvement vs. placebo of 34% (median = 48%) in season 3 (4-month pre-seasonal treatment group). In this group, the mean AAdSS±SD was 3.79±3.95 in monosensitized patients and 3.31±3.49 in polysensitized patients. The treatment effect seemed to appear at lower pollen levels in the 2nd and 3rd seasons (booster effect). Treatment-related adverse events were mostly transient and mild to moderate in intensity, and their number decreased in the 2nd and 3rd treatment seasons. Conclusion: Three years of pre-coseasonal treatment with a 300IR 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet showed a sustained effect with statistical and clinically significant improvement of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms in adults and a booster effect was observed. Efficacy was good in mono and in polysensitized patients. A potentially disease-modifying effect is now being investigated by discontinuing the SLIT and scoring the patients' symptoms for 2 additional seasons.
Efficacy and safety of timothy grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in North American adults; Background: Until now, the efficacy of grass sublingual immunotherapy has not been demonstrated in North America. This phase III trial investigated the efficacy and safety of daily administration of grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) (oral lyophilisate, Phleum pratense, 2800 BAU) in allergic rhinocon-junctivitis (AR) subjects with or without asthma. Methods: 439 adults with Timothy grass pollen-induced AR were randomized 1:1 to once-daily grass AIT or placebo for approximately 16 weeks before and during the 2009 grass pollen season (GPS). The primary efficacy endpoint comprised the average total combined daily symptom and medication score (TCS) during the entire GPS. Key secondary endpoints were individual daily symptom score (DSS), daily medication score (DMS), and Rhinocon-junctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ[S]) with standardized activities. Carbamylated monoid allergoids as a new therapeutic option for sublingual immunotherapy of mite- and grass-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis - A systematic review of published trials using Lais® tablets; Lais® allergoid tablets contain allergens, which are modified by carbamylation. Due to their modified chemical structure they are suitable for sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). Based on their small molecule size of 12-40 kDa, they can be absorbed easily via the oral mucosa. In this review, the efficacy of SLIT with carbamylated monoid allergoid tablets on the treatment of grass pollen- and mite-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis was studied on the basis of symptom score and medication score improvement. Following a selective internet and databank search, six trials - in part also placebo-controlled - on the treatment of grass pollen- (n = 266) and mite-induced (n = 241) allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were suitable for conclusions regarding the clinical efficacy of allergoid tablets. The primary endpoints in these trials were the decrease in the need for antiall ergic medication and/or the reduction in the occurrence of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. Following data concerning symptoms and medication recorded in patient diaries, conclusions could be made about the effectiveness and tolerance of Lais® tablets. The average improvement of the symptom score for three trials on the treatment of grass pollen all ergy was 34% in comparison to improvement under placebo. For the treatment of mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis, an average symptom score improvement of 22% became apparent compared to the placebo or control group. The intake of symptomatic PRN medication under therapy with allergoid tablets declined during the course of therapy. Under treatment of grass pollen allergy, the medication score improved by an average of 49% and by 24% in the treatment of mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis as opposed to placebo or control. Only few side effects have been documented in trials and predominantly local effects have been observed. Severe systemic side effects did not occur. On the basis of the trial results summarized in this review, it can be suggested that SLIT with Lais® sublingual tablets is an effective and well-tolerated form of treatment.
Carbamylated monomelic allergoids as a therapeutic option for sublingual immunotherapy of dust mite- and grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis: A systematic review of published trials with a meta-analysis of treatment using Lais® tablets; Lais® allergoid tablets contain allergens that are modified by carbamylation. Due to their modified chemical structure, they are suitable for sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) (13, 16, 17, 24). Based on their small molecule size of 12 to 40 kDa, they can be easily absorbed via the oral mucosa (1). In this review, we studied the efficacy of SLIT with carbamylated monomeric allergoid tablets in the treatment of grass pollen- and dust mite-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis on the basis of symptom and medication score improvements. Following a selective internet and databank search, six trials - some placebo-controlled - regarding the treatment of grass pollen- (n = 266) and dust mite-induced (n = 241) allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were used to draw conclusions regarding the clinical efficacy of allergoid tablets. The primary endpoints in these trials were decreases in the need for allergy medications and/or reductions in the occurrence of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. Data was recorded from patient diaries regarding their symptoms and medications used and conclusions were then drawn about the effectiveness of and tolerance to Lais® tablets. The average improvement in symptom score in three trials of grass pollen allergy treatment was 34% in comparison to the placebo group. The treatment of dust mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis produced an average symptom score improvement of 22% compared to the placebo or control groups. The intake of symptomatic PRN medication during allergoid tablet therapy declined. Treatment of grass pollen allergies and dust mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis showed an average medication score improvement of 49% and 24%, respectively. Few side effects were documented in the trials and predominantly local effects were observed. Severe systemic side effects did not occur. On the basis of the trial results summarized in this review, we suggest that SLIT using Lais® sublingual tablets is an effective and well-tolerated form of treatment.
FcεRI levels and frequencies of peripheral blood dendritic cell populations in allergic rhinitis; The dendritic cell (DC) lineage encompasses a diverse population of cells with unique subtype-specific functions. In peripheral blood, four DC subsets have been identified based on their distinct expression of CD1c, CD141, CD16, and CD123, and these subpopulations exhibit functional properties in immune responses. However, their respective roles in allergic diseases, such as rhinitis, are unclear. In this study, we have performed comparative assessments of DC subset frequencies and investigated their FcεRI expression levels in patients with allergic rhinitis. We demonstrate that the frequencies of CD1c+ and CD141+ DCs are elevated in grass pollen-allergic subjects compared with healthy controls, irrespectively of allergen stimulation. Among the DC subsets, CD1c+ DCs expressed the highest levels of FcεRI mRNA, and a large proportion expressed surface FcεRI. Furthermore, the FcεRI expression levels were augmented upon allergen challenge. Thus our data suggest that CD1c+ DCs influence allergen-specific immune responses. Research on their functional properties in allergy is warranted for development of future immunotherapies targeting specialized DC subsets. © 2010 American Society for Histocompatibility and Immunogenetics.
Five-grass pollen 300IR SLIT tablets: Efficacy and safety in children and adolescents; The efficacy and safety of five-grass pollen 300IR sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets (Stallergènes SA, France) have previously been demonstrated in paediatric patients. This report presents additional data concerning efficacy at pollen peak, efficacy and safety according to age, nasal and ocular symptoms, use of rescue medication, satisfaction with treatment and compliance. Children (5-11 yr) and adolescents (12-17 yr) with grass pollen-allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were included in a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study and received either a 300IR five-grass pollen tablet or placebo daily in a pre- (4 months) and co-seasonal protocol. The severity of six symptoms (sneezing, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, nasal and ocular pruritis, and tearing) was scored, and rescue medication use was recorded daily during the pollen season. Patient satisfaction was recorded at the season end. A total of 161 children and 117 adolescents were evaluated (n = 267). 300IR SLIT was effective over the whole season (p = 0.0010) and at the pollen peak (p = 0.0009). The adjusted mean difference between 300IR and placebo groups was significant for both nasal (p = 0.0183) and ocular (p < 0.0001) symptoms. Rescue medication use was statistically lower in the SLIT group during the pollen season and at the pollen peak (both p < 0.05). More patients in the SLIT group were satisfied with their treatment compared to placebo (83.2% vs. 68.1%, p = 0.0030), and compliance was high (SLIT 93.9% of patients were compliant, placebo 94.8% of patients were compliant). SLIT was well tolerated by children and adolescents. 300IR five-grass pollen tablets are effective and safe during the pollen season and at the pollen peak in children and adolescents with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis. © 2010 John Wiley & Sons AS.
Bridging allergologic and botanical knowledge in seasonal allergy: A role for phenology; Background Grass pollen is a worldwide cause of respiratory allergy. Identifying the causative species is essential, for example for choosing the appropriate immunotherapy, because not all grass allergens are totally cross-reacting, and the pollen calendars provide only a gross estimate. Phenologic analyses allow identification of the pollen release for each individual grass. Objectives To assess, using phenologic analyses, the true flowering periods of grasses and to compare the data with the standard pollen calendar. Methods Phenologic analyses were performed of the following grasses: black grass, sweet vernal grass, common wild oat, barren brome, cocksfoot, tall fescue, Yorkshire fog, ryegrass, Timothy grass, bulbous meadow-grass, Kentucky bluegrass, and Bermuda grass. Sampling was performed every 10 days, starting in April 2009, at 50 stations distributed across Italy. The flowering phase was assessed using a stereomicroscopy-based method for the detection of spreading stamens. The official pollen calendar was used for comparison. Results Relevant differences were found between grass pollen count and effective flowering of the grass species. Only some species contributed to the pollen peak, and a relevant pollen load for other species was also present out of the peak. Important Pooideae, such as Timothy grass, were not present during the pollen peak in northern and central Italy, and the same occurred with Bermuda grass. Conclusions The various species of grasses release their pollen grains at different times during the pollen season, and this information is missing with pollen calendars. This may have a relevant effect on the choice of an appropriate immunotherapy. © 2010 American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.
Grass pollen allergy in Queensland: How important are the subtropical grass pollens for triggering allergic rhinitis and asthma?; Grass pollen allergens are major triggers of allergic rhinitis and asthma. Treatment of grass pollen allergy by immunotherapy in school children reduces the subsequent risk of asthma but most reagents for diagnosis and immunotherapy are based on pollens of cool climate grass pollens. We aim to determine the frequency of IgE reactivity with temperate and subtropical grass pollens in patients with grass pollen allergy in Brisbane and to assess IgE cross-reactivity amongst the different grass pollens. IgE reactivity with pollen extracts of subtropical Bahia, Johnson and Bermuda grasses compared with pollen allergens of temperate Ryegrass was tested in 58 healthy control donors, 47 grass pollen-allergic donors, 33 donors with equivocal grass pollen-allergy by skin prick testing and 33 donors with sensitivity to allergens other than grass pollen. Patients with grass pollen allergy in Brisbane showed similarly high levels and frequency of IgE reactivity with each type of grass pollen. There was a greater correlation between IgE reactivity amongst subtropical grass pollens Abstracts than between subtropical and temperate ryegrass pollens. Cross-inhibition ELISA with four individual patients revealed species-specific -Ig reactivity with Bahia, Johnson, Bermuda and Ryegrass pollen that was not fully blocked by other grass pollen allergens indicating that patient IgE recognized differently grass pollen allergens from separate botanical subfamilies. Subtropical grass pollens are important allergens for patients in Brisbane with allergic rhinitis and asthma. The pattern of IgE reactivity in patients with grass pollen allergy in Brisbane is distinct from that of patients with grass pollen allergy in Melbourne who previously showed significantly lower IgE reactivity with subtropical grass pollens than temperate grass pollens. Knowledge of sensitization to subtropical grass pollen allergens will provide guidelines for clinical practice on appropriate grass pollen allergen immunotherapy for improved treatment efficacy and reduction of the burden of allergic rhinitis and risk of asthma.
Which allergen extract for grass pollen immunotherapy an in vitro study; Background: Grass pollen is a major cause of allergy throughout the world. The only treatment targeting the causes and not only the symptoms of allergy is specific immunotherapy (IT). A number of controlled trials demonstrated the efficacy of IT in grass pollen allergic subjects, most using extracts of multiple grasses but some using extracts of a single grass. The optimal grass extract for IT has not yet been established. Methods: This study is aimed at investigating the IgE-binding pattern in sera from IT-nave patients from central Italy with allergic rhinitis andor asthma caused by grass pollen. A 5-grass extract was used (containing Dactylis glomerata, Poa pratensis, Lolium perenne, Antoxanthum odoratum and Phleum pratense) and compared to Phleum pratense alone, which is the most frequently used single grass extract, by the RAST-inhibition technique. Results: The 5-grass extract showed, by RAST-inhibition, a significantly higher binding compared to the Phleum pratense extract for Antoxanthum odoratum and Poa pratensis, while the two extracts for immunotherapy showed similar binding affinity for Phleum pratense and the non-Pooideae grass, Cynodon dactylon. Conclusions: The use of a mixed-grass pollen extract seems to be the optimal choice when applying specific IT in grass pollen-allergic subjects from the Mediterranean area. © 2010 Informa UK, Ltd.
Molecular determinants of T cell epitope recognition to the common Timothy grass allergen; We investigated the molecular determinants of allergen-derived T cell epitopes in humans utilizing the Phleum pratense (Timothy grass) allergens (Phl p). PBMCs from allergic individuals were tested in ELISPOT assays with overlapping peptides spanning known Phl p allergens. A total of 43 distinct antigenic regions were recognized, illustrating the large breadth of grass-specific T cell epitopes. Th2 cytokines (as represented by IL-5) were predominant, whereas IFN-γ, IL-10, and IL-17 were detected less frequently. Responses from specific immunotherapy treatment individuals were weaker and less consistent, yet similar in epitope specificity and cytokine pattern to allergic donors, whereas nonallergic individuals were essentially nonreactive. Despite the large breadth of recognition, nine dominant antigenic regions were defined, each recognized by multiple donors, accounting for 51% of the total response. Multiple HLA molecules and loci restricted the dominant regions, and the immunodominant epitopes could be predicted using bioinformatic algorithms specific for 23 common HLA-DR, DP, and DQ molecules. Immunodominance was also apparent at the Phl p Ag level. It was found that 52, 19, and 14% of the total response was directed to Phl p 5, 1, and 3, respectively. Interestingly, little or no correlation between Phl p-specific IgE levels and T cell responses was found. Thus, certain intrinsic features of the allergen protein might influence immunogenicity at the level of T cell reactivity. Consistent with this notion, different Phl p Ags were associated with distinct patterns of IL-5, IFN-γ, IL-10, and IL-17 production. Copyright © 2010 by The American Association of Immunologists, Inc.
Allergen immunotherapy in Iceland 1977-2006; INTRODUCTION: The prevelance of allery and asthma has increased rapidly over the last 3 decades and is now estimated that 25-30% of population in Western industrialized countries show symptoms of allergy or asthma. The aim of this study was to reveal the success of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) in Landspitali from 1977-2006. MATERIAL AND METHODS: During the study period a total number of 289 individuals underwent immunotherapy in outpatient clinic of allergy and asthma in Landspítali. A total number of 169 individuals were contacted, of whom 128 (76%) accepted to participate in the study. The evaluation was based on medical records, standardized questionnaire and skin-prick tests. RESULTS: Patients were evaluated on the average of 20 years after finishing treatment. 118 (92%) patients were desensitized to grass pollen, to birch pollen (30%), cat dander (30%) and dust mite (28%). At the time of the study 67% reported to be asymptomatic or with greatly improved allergy symptoms. Males had better response to AIT than women (p=0.04). Participants with positive family history of allergy and/or asthma in first degree relatives also reported better response to AIT (p=0.02). Furthermore, AIT to grass pollen and dust mite seemed to be more effective than AIT to cat dander and birch (p=0.04). AIT was also shown to reduce asthma. CONCLUSION: AIT for 3-5 years provides significant beneficial effect of allergy and asthma symptoms in patients who undergo such therapy. Finally, it s findings support the notion that AIT may reduce the risk of new allergic manifestations.
Tolerance induction after specific immunotherapy with pollen allergoids adjuvanted by monophosphoryl lipid A in children; Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is a well-established and clinically effective treatment for allergic diseases. A pollen allergoid formulated with the T helper type 1 (Th1)-inducing adjuvant monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL) facilitates short-term SIT. Little is known about mechanisms of tolerance induction in this setting. In a prospective study, 34 patients allergic to grass pollen (25 male, nine female, median age 10·2 years) received a total of 44 SIT courses (20 in the first, 24 in the second) with MPL-adjuvanted pollen allergoids. Immunogenicity was measured by levels of specific immunoglobulin G (IgG grass) and IgG4grass by antibody blocking properties on basophil activation, and by induction of CD4+, CD25+ and forkhead box P3 (FoxP3+) regulatory T cells (Treg). Specific IgG and IgG4 levels increased only slightly in the first year of SIT. In the second year these changes reached significance (P < 0·0001). In keeping with these findings, we were able to show an increase of T reg cells and a decreased release of leukotrienes after the second year of treatment. In the first year of treatment we found little evidence for immunological changes. A significant antibody induction was seen only after the second course of SIT. Short-course immunotherapy with pollen allergoids formulated with the Th1-inducing adjuvant MPL needs at least two courses to establish tolerance. © 2010 British Society for Immunology.
The biological potency of different extracts for sublingual immunotherapy assessed by skin prick tests; The standardization of allergen extracts is of primary relevance to the clinical efficacy. Biological standardization procedures are widely used in the commercial production of vaccines. We tested, in grass-allergic patients, the potency of three different grass extracts for sublingual immunotherapy by means of skin prick tests. Specific IgE against Phl p 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12 were also assayed. Allerslit® and Sublivac® were directly applied as skin test. Grazax®, was prepared by dissolving two tablets in 2mL saline. Thirty-three subjects (mean age 38.8) were studied. The skin response was significantly different among extracts, decreasing from Allerslit to Grazax (t test <0.01), but all the extract produced a skin response greater than histamine. All the subjects had specific IgE to Phl p 1 and Phl p 4 but 24% did not have specific IgE to Phl p 5. In those subjects the skin response to the three extracts did not differ from that of Phl p 5-positive subjects. Our findings confirm that there is a variability in the biological potency among different extracts. In addition, the standardization of grass extracts based on Phl p 5 only, may be insufficient in some cases.
Subcutaneous immunotherapy with a preparation with optimised allergen aluminium hydroxide ratio: A randomised parallel-group clinical trial investigating safety and tolerability; Background: For subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) allergens usually are adsorbed to aluminium hydroxide (alum) for slow allergen release (depot effect). In addition alum also acts as an adjuvant that enhances the immunological effect. Therefore, a SCIT product with an optimised allergen/alum ratio allows for reducing the maximum dose applied for maintenance therapy and shorter up-dosing schedules. In a clinical trial safety and tolerability profile of a product with an optimised allergen/alum ratio has been investigated. Methods: In a randomised, controlled, parallel-group trial patients with rhinoconjunctivitis with/without asthma induced by grass pollen were treated with a SCIT depot preparation (four grasses and rye, AVANZ, ALK-Abello, Hørsholm, Denmark) containing 15% of the allergen content and 50% of the alum content compared with the widely used ALK allergen product for SCIT (Alutard SQ, ALK-Abelló, Hørsholm, Denmark). Therapy was initiated utilising an up-dosing phase with five injections (300, 600, 3000, 6000, 15 000 SQ+) with weekly intervals in group 1 and 3-4 days intervals in group 2 and was continued by two maintenance injections of 15 000 SQ+ with 14 and 28 days intervals. Results: In total 400 patients were treated (group 1: 201, group 2: 199) with the five injection up-dosing schedule. The trial was completed according to the injection schedule by 358 patients (group 1: 185, group 2: 173). Fewer local and systemic reactions were observed during up-dosing with one week intervals (group 1) compared with 3-4 days intervals (group 2). Local reactions were observed in group 1 in 68/201 patients (33.8%) and 93/199 (46.7%) patients in group 2. Delayed systemic reactions (1 h after the injection or later) occurred in 41/201 (20.4%) patients in group 1 and 63/199 (31.7%) patients in group 2 predominantly as rhinoconjunctivits or urticaria. The frequency of local and systemic reactions was much lower for the two maintenance injections in both treatment groups. Conclusion: Using a five injections up-dosing schedule a SCIT product with an optimised allergen/adjuvant ratio (AVANZ) was found to be well tolerated. Fewer local and systemic reactions were observed for up-dosing with injection intervals of 1 week compared with 3-4 days injection intervals.
Effect of birch pollen specific immunotherapy on birch pollen-related hazelnut allergy; Background: Birch pollen allergy can lead to pollen-related hazelnut allergy, due to cross-reactivity via the major allergens in birch (Bet v 1) and hazelnut (Cor a 1). However, it is unclear whether birch pollen specific immunotherapy (SIT) can be used to treat the associated hazelnut allergy. Objective: To evaluate the effect of birch pollen SIT on clinical and immunological parameters of birch pollen and hazelnut allergy. Methods: In a double-blind study, nineteen patients with birch pollen allergy and concomitant hazelnut allergy were randomly assigned to 1 year subcutaneous birch pollen SIT (Alutard SQ, ALK-Abelló) or placebo-treatment (histamine). Reactions upon accidental hazelnut ingestion during the treatment period were recorded in diaries. Eliciting doses for hazelnut and symptoms (visual analogue scale) were determined by double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge (DBPCFC) before and after 1 year of treatment. Titrated skin prick tests were performed using birch pollen and hazelnut extract, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1, before and at various time points after treatment. Grass pollen, house dust mite and cat extract were used as control allergens. IgE, IgG4 and IgG levels in serum were measured for birch pollen and hazelnut extract, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1. In addition, the effect of SIT on IgE-facilitated allergen binding (IgE-FAB) was measured by flow cytometry. Results: Hazelnut eliciting doses and symptoms measured by VAS during DBPCFC did not change upon treatment in the SIT or the placebo group. Reactions upon accidental hazelnut ingestion were less frequently reported in the SIT group. In the SIT group, skin prick test responses to birch pollen, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1, but not to control allergens, decreased significantly upon treatment. Serum levels of IgG4 and IgG towards birch pollen and Bet v 1, and IgG towards Cor a 1, showed a significant increase. IgE-FAB was inhibited to a significantly larger extent for all allergens in the SIT group than in the placebo group. Conclusion: No objective clinical improvement of hazelnut allergy was observed by DBPCFC, though reported reactions upon accidental ingestions were less frequent. Birch pollen SIT induced significant changes in skin prick test, IgG responses and IgE-FAB towards Bet v 1 and the cross-reactive allergen Cor a 1. This indicates that birch pollen SIT may be useful to treat the associated hazelnut allergy, but a higher dose or prolonged treatment may be necessary.
ImmunoCAP ISAC IgE and IgG4 as tools for monitoring specific immunotherapy; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is an effective treatment of pollen allergy. However, its effect on pollen-related food allergy remains unclear. Specific (s) IgE and IgG4 can be measured during SIT to monitor immunological effect and perhaps to predict treatment efficacy, but its usefulness have been hampered by the lack of component-specific antibody tests. Methods: Sera from eight allergic patients treated with conventional birch (n = 8) and timothy pollen (n = 6) SIT, and three non-treated controls, were analyzed using ImmunoCAP ISAC® IgE and IgG4, novel assays that allows semi-quantitative measurements of IgE and IgG4 antibodies against 103 allergenic components simultaneously. Results: All eight SIT-patients had IgE, and 5 had IgG4, to Bet v 1 from birch at baseline. Common was also IgE to Cor a 1.04 (hazelnut) and Mal d 4 (apple) and IgG4 to Api g 1 (celery). Median number of sensitizations to the 11 PR-10 allergens included was 5.5 (range: 2-9). The corresponding figure for sIgG4 was 2 (range: 0-8). The IgE levels to Bet v 1 decreased for 7 SIT-patients at 1st and 2nd BPS (median decrease from baseline: 76%, range: 53%-89%) while IgG4 dramatically increased in all 8 during SIT (median increase: 725%, range: 34%-7450%). Of the 6 patients treated with grass-SIT, IgE to Phl p 1 (n = 5) and Phl p 5 (n = 3) was most common at baseline. Generally, the sIgE levels fell during SIT. Only one SIT-patient had IgE to the five profilins included and none had IgE to the two polcalcins (cross-reactive panallergens) at baseline. One had low levels of IgG4 to the profilins and polcalcins at baseline. Three patients developed new sensitizations to profilins. In two of them, IgG4 was developed against the same allergen components. Altogether, three negative SIT-patients developed IgG4 to most profilins and polcalcins and one patient developed IgG4 to all profilins except Phl p 12. Conclusion: ImmunoCAP ISAC IgE and IgG4 offer new possibilities to study detailed serological changes during SIT.

Decreased maturation of human oral mucosal dendritic cells compared to epidermal dendritic cells upon binding of birch and grass pollen allergen; Background: Allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT) remains the only effective causal treatment for allergic rhinitis. The invasive character of subcutaneous immunotherapy and severe systemic adverse reactions enforced the search for novel, non-invasive applications strategies. In this regard sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) has been shown to be a safe and effective alternative. Further on, recently published data could demonstrate safety and efficacy of epicutaneous application of grass pollen allergen. The induction of allergen-specific regulatory T cells (Tregs) has been postulated as an important immunological mechanism of AIT. Without much doubt, local antigen-presenting cells such oral mucosal dendritic cells (oDCs) or epidermal DCs (eDCs) are critical as they are able to induce Tregs. The current paradigm postulates that in contrast to mature DCs, immature DCs preferentially induce tolerance. However, only little is known about the impact of allergen uptake by oDCs and eDCs on their maturation state. For this reason, resorption of the allergen Bet v1 or Phlp 5 and their impact on the maturation of human oDC as compared to eDCs was studied in an ex vivo model. Methods: Human oral mucosal and epidermal biopsies were placed on petri-dishes and incubated at 4°C and 37°C with PBS containing 100 μg/ml FITC-coupled Phlp 5 or Bet v1. After 1 h of incubation, tissue was washed with PBS and placed in medium at 37°C for DC migration. Maturation state of CD1a+ DCs was analysed after 36 h, measuring CD83 and CCR7 expression. Results: While migration of eDCs from epidermis previously stimulated with Phl p5 led to full maturation of eDCs reflected by induction of CD83 and lymph node homing receptor CCR7 expression, migrated oDCs displayed only reduced expression of maturation marker CD83 and little amounts of CCR7. Most interestingly, oDCs bound to allergen displayed significantly lower expression of CD83 and CCR7 compared to oDCs, which did not bind any allergen. Conclusion: Binding of allergen to eDCs leads to their full maturation, while maturation of oDCs was inhibited, which might have an impact on their tolerogenic properties during AIT.
Application of mass spectrometry to the characterisation and quantification of pharmaceutical-grade allergens; Background: Structural characterization and accurate quantification of major allergens are needed to support the development of high-quality products for specific immunotherapy. Herein, we investigate the pertinence of mass spectrometry (MS) to establish primary structure, monitor structural modifications and obtain quantitative data on major allergens. Methods: Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) and high resolution/high mass accuracy electrospray (ESI) MS were combined to determine the primary sequence variations of relevant mite, grass or birch pollen allergens. Purified allergens were analyzed either as intact proteins or following reduction, alkylation and tryptic digestion. Liquid chromatography (LC)-ESI-MS/MS was applied to the detection of species-specific isoforms and quantification of grass pollen group 1 allergens. To this aim 3 target tryptic peptides were monitored in comparison with synthetic peptides labeled with [13C6,15N]Leu and [13C9,15N]Phe used for calibration. Results: In a first MS study, group 1 pollen allergens from five different Pooideae species were shown to exhibit significant intra-and inter-species primary sequence variability. They also displayed variations in proline hydroxylation, N-glycosylation motifs and O-glycosylation. Two MS-assays were consequently developed to monitor a five grass mix vaccine, namely (i) an identity test detecting species-specific group 1-derived peptides, that demonstrated the presence of components from all species in the mix and (ii) an assay for quantifying all the group 1 isoforms, that confirmed batch consistency. In a second study, variants of the house dust mite allergen Der p 2 were characterized in pharmaceutical-grade material, showing the relative contribution of Der p 2.0101, 2.0105, 2.0109 and 2.0110 isoforms. In a third MS study, a recombinant Bet v 1α product intended for a phase III clinical trial was characterized. Primary structure was entirely confirmed as well as low levels of degradation products. Conclusion: MS represents a very suitable approach for in-depth characterization and quantification of pharmaceutical grade relevant allergens intended for specific immunotherapy.

Sensitisation to birch, timothy grass and peanut allergen components in patients from the south-east region of Norway; Background: To assess the sensitization profile in pollen allergic patients using allergenic components can be helpful before starting allergen-specific immunotherapy. Pollen allergic patients in Northern Europe, unlike in the South, are mostly sensitized to major birch allergen Bet v 1 and to grass allergens Phl p 1 and 5b. In accordance with this, occurrence of birch pollen-related peanut sensitization is expected to be high. Response to pollen immunotherapy in local allergic rhinitis; Background: Patients with local allergic rhinitis (LAR) present in situ synthesis of specific-IgE and nasal inflammatory response induced by aeroallergens. Methods: Twenty adult patients with grass pollen LAR were included in an open observational study. Ten patients were treated with subcutaneous SIT with grass during 6 months and with symptomatic treatment (antihistamine and/or intranasal corticoteroids) and the other ten patients with symptomatic treatment only. Efficacy endpoints comprised response to NAPT-grass, SPT, symptoms and medication scores. Serum and nasal lavage samples were freezed to further studies. Results: In the active group NAPT-grass was negative in three patients after 6 month-SIT, and the others seven needed 50 or 100 times more allergen to achieve a positive response. SPT became positive to grass in four patients after 6 month. Symptoms and medication scores showed important decreases in the next spring (70% and 80% respectively). No adverse effects were detected. In the control group no differences were found in NAPT-grass, SPT, symptom and medication scores. Conclusions: Treatment with SIT with grass induced increase of tolerance to the aeroallergen, reduction of symptoms and rescue medication in LAR patients. Conversion from negative to positive SPT may indicate that LAR can be a first step in the natural evolution toward allergic rhinitis. Follow-up and double-blind pacebo-controlled studies are needed to prove the efficacy and safety of SIT in subject with LAR.

Safety of sublingual immunotherapy for treatment of patients with severe asthma; Introduction: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) has been established as an effective treatment for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in adults, with fewer reported systemic adverse reactions than subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). Definitive evidence for a benefit of SLIT in the treatment asthma is emerging. Currently patients with the most severe asthma (FEV1 < 70% predicted) are excluded from receiving immunotherapy (IMT) in trials and clinical practice guidelines. To date, no data has been published regarding the safety of SLIT in these patients. We describe a series of nine patients with postbronchodilator FEV1 of between 30 and 66% predicted who have received SLIT for several indications. Methods: Nine patients receiving SLIT with an FEV1 < 70% predicted prior to starting IMT were identified from pharmacy, hospital and departmental databases at three sites. There were five female and four male patients identified, with ages ranging from 33 to 65 years. Allergens used included house dust mite (HDM) only (five patients), HDM and grass pollen (three patients), and HDM, grass pollen and cat dander (one patient). Clinician interviews and retrospective review of medical records were undertaken to assess for occurrence of side effects, which were graded according to the recommendations of published guidelines for standardisation of IMT trials. Data regarding treatment interruption and increase in asthma rescue medication use was also collected. Results: No systemic side effects were reported in any of the nine patients. No patients required treatment interruption or modification as a consequence of any adverse reactions to SLIT. Asthma rescue medication use was not increased in any of the patients. Conclusion: In this highly selected group of nine patients with FEV1 < 70% predicted, SLIT has been safely administered without any systemic side effects or exacerbations of asthma as assessed by rescue medication use. Further prospective studies are warranted to investigate the safety of SLIT in the population with FEV1 < 70% predicted.

Optimised allergen: Adjuvant ratio potentiates immunogenicity of AlOH-formulated Phleum pratense extract; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) administered either subcutaneously (SCIT) or sublingually in the form of Allergy Immunotherapy Tablets (AIT) have proven sustained clinical efficacy against grass-pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. While grass AIT can be initiated directly with the recommended maintenance dose of allergen, gradual updosing over a period of weeks is the recommended regimen for SCIT. Commonly, in commercial products for SCIT the specific allergen is formulated with an adjuvant, most often in the form of aluminium hydroxide (AlOH). The mechanism behind the therapeutic effect of SIT is not completely known. However, it has been shown that allergen-specific IgG antibodies are induced after successful SIT. Here we investigate the possibility of optimising the formulation of AlOH-based grass-pollen allergy vaccines for SCIT in a way that allows for shorter updosing regimens while maintaining the immunogenicity of the vaccine. Methods: Mice were immunised every second week with a conventionally formulated vaccine containing a maintenance dose of 20 kSQ Phl p extract adsorbed to 0.228 mg AlOH, a diluted maintenance dose of 3 kSQ Phl p extract adsorbed to 0.034 mg AlOH or an alternative formulation that consisted of 3 kSQ Phl p extract in the maintenance dose adsorbed to 0.114 mg AlOH. Kinetics of Phl p specific IgG1 antibody responses in serum were quantified. Allergenicity, measured as the ability of the formulations to activate human basophils, was also determined. Results: There were no differences in Phl p-specific IgG1 antibody responses between the groups immunised with either 20 kSQ Phl p + 0.228 mg AlOH or 3 kSQ Phl p + 0.114 mg AlOH. However, immunisation with the new alternative formulation with 3 kSQ Phl p extract + 0.114 mg gave rise to significantly higher IgG1 antibody responses as compared to the group immunised with 3 kSQ Phl p extract + 0.034 mg AlOH. The allergenicity of the 3 kSQ Phl p + 0.114 mg AlOH formulation was 5-20 fold reduced as compared to the 20 kSQ Phl p + 0.228 mg AlOH formulation. Conclusions: The optimisation of the ratio between allergen and adjuvant allows for administration of a lower dose of allergen while maintaining the immunogenicity of the product and at the same time reducing the allergenicity. This study indicates that the optimisation of the ratio between the allergen and the adjuvant could benefit the safety/efficacy profile and allow for shorter updosing.

Recombinant hypoallergenic variants of Phl p 5: Candidates for allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: Group 5 allergens are major allergens of grasses. Together with group 1 allergens they account for the majority of IgE-reactivity in sera of grass pollen-allergic subjects. Recombinant Timothy grass (Phleum pratense) Phl p 5a and Phl p 5b have already been used in clinical trials of allergen-specific immunotherapy as part of a cocktail of natively folded recombinant allergens. The development of hypoallergenic allergens should further improve allergen-specific immunotherapy by reducing the risk of anaphylactic reactions at increased therapeutic dosage. Methods: A set of variants of Phl p 5 with mutations at proline sites were constructed and expressed in E. coli. The purified proteins were compared with physicochemical methods such as SDS-PAGE, UV/vis-spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and multiple angle light-scattering, as well as immunological methods such as IgE-binding assays, basophil activation tests and T-cell stimulation assays. Results: The mutation of proline residues preferably located in loops connecting adjacent α-helices resulted in molecules with decreased IgE-binding. A strong reduction of IgE-binding could be achieved by combining multiple proline mutations. However, some proline residues were found to be crucial for maintaining solubility or homogeneity of those variants. Deletion of P211 always resulted in aggregation, whereas substitution of P211 with leucine yielded soluble hypoallergenic molecules. Maintaining the prolines P146 and P155 yielded pure monomeric preparations, whereas deletion of these residues resulted in a mixture of monomers and dimers. Selected candidates with excellent physicochemical characteristics proved to be both hypoallergenic and T-cell reactive. Conclusion: The hypoallergenic Phl p 5 variant with deletions of prolines at position 57, 58, 117, 180 and 229 and a substitution of proline 211 with leucine is an excellent candidate for allergen-specific immunotherapy. This variant can be produced with high yield in E. coli and the purified protein meets the high demands made for recombinant therapeutics.
Recombinant hypoallergenic variants of Phl p 6: Candidates for allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: Phl p 6 is a major allergen of Timothy grass (Phleum pratense). Group 6 allergens have been found only in Timothy and Kentucky blue grass so far. However, despite the observed structural similarity of Phl p 6 and the Phl p 5 N-terminus, immunological differences resulting from unique Phl p 6 epitopes can be observed. Therefore recombinant Phl p 6 has been used in clinical trials of allergen-specific immunotherapy as part of a cocktail of recombinant allergens with native fold. Hypoallergenic variants are believed to further improve allergen-specific immunotherapy. Methods: A set of variants of Phl p 6 with mutations at proline sites were constructed and expressed in E. coli. The purified proteins were compared with physicochemical methods such as SDS-PAGE, UV/vis-spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and multiple angle light-scattering, as well as immunological methods such as IgE-binding assays, basophil activation tests and T-cell stimulation assays. Results: The mutation of proline residues preferably located in loops connecting adjacent α-helices resulted in molecules with decreased IgE-binding. Deletion of proline 29 and 30 proved to have the strongest effect on IgE-reactivity, whereas the mutation of proline 101 had almost no effect. A further reduction of IgE-binding could be obtained by combining multiple proline mutations. Combining deletions of P29 and P30 with mutations of P57 and/or P79 showed a strong hypoallergenic effect. Combination mutants that carry a modification of P57 were found to consist of a mixture of monomers and dimers. In contrast those mutations that maintain P57 and have mutations at P79 are monomeric molecules with excellent physicochemical and hypoallergenic characteristics. Conclusion: A hypoallergenic Phl p 6 variant with mutations of prolines at position 29, 30 and 79 is an excellent candidate for allergen-specific immunotherapy. This variant can be produced with high yield in E. coli and the purified protein meets the high demands made for recombinant therapeutics.

Lack of association between clinical efficacy and cellular immune responses in the blood during grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: The efficacy of a 300-IR 5-grass-pollen SLIT tablet on rhinoconjonctivitis symptoms was confirmed in a double blind, placebo controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber (ACC). We took advantage of this study to inquire whether changes in basophil activation and T cell responses can be used as biomarkers predicting efficacy. Methods: Changes in immunological markers were investigated in 82 patients with grass pollen-related allergic rhinoconjunctivitis who received active or placebo tablets sublingually once a day for four months. An allergen challenge with grass pollen was performed in the Vienna Challenge Chamber (VCC) at baseline, after 1 week, and after 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment. Blood samples were collected before treatment and after 2 and 4 treatment months for assessment of basophil activation (based on CD203c expression) and T cell responses (looking at proliferation, pheno-type, cytokine production and gene expression). Results: SLIT with a 5-grass-pollen tablet led to significant improvement (versus placebo) of 29.8% for the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) at end point. Clinical responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. No changes in basophil activation and T-cell proliferation were noticed for active and placebo groups in response to either the extract, Dac g 1 or Dac g 5 allergens, during treatment. Higher expression of Treg markers (eg Foxp 3) and lower expression of molecules associated with a Th1/Th2 profile were observed during treatment for both active and placebo groups. PMBCs from patients exposed to active treatment (versus placebo) displayed a lower production of TNF-alpha and a higher expression of IFN-gamma, with no differences between responders and non responders. All patients with a high symptom score before treatment responded to SLIT. However, neither basophil activation nor levels of T cell proliferation prior to treatment were predictive of efficacy. Conclusion: Basophil activation and T cell responses measured in the blood are not predictive of clinical responses induced by SLIT. Our results do not preclude that changes in cellular responses monitored in target respiratory mucosae can account for SLIT efficacy.
Development of experimental hyposensitisation with timothy grass pollen extract in adjuvant-free IgE-mediated murine model of asthma; Background: Bronchial asthma (BA) is widespread chronic respiratory disorder. Allergen-specific immunotherapy (ASIT) is one of most common ways of BA treatment. ASIT reduces sensitization and bronchial hyperresponsiviness (BHR). Therefore the aim of our study was to develop the model of experimental hyposensitization (EH) exploiting the timothy grass pollen extract (G6) on the adjuvant-free IgE-mediated murine model of asthma (MMA) and to test the efficacy of new approaches of ASIT in G6-connected allergic conditions. Methods: Timothy grass pollen extract (G6) was obtained by standard methodology and standardized in protein content. Female BALB/c mice were systemically sensitized (SS) by seven intraperitoneal (i/ p) injections on the other day with 1 mg/ kg of G6 in 0.5 ml of saline. Forty-nine days later mice were challenged with 8 daily intranasal applications (INA) of 50 μl G6 extract in concentration 10 mg/ml of G6. Experimental ASIT was performed within the interval between SS and INA by treatment of mice with G6 extract using 16 subcutaneous (s/c) injections of increasing doses (in protein content): 0.05 mg/kg (four injections), 0.5 mg/kg (four injections), 5 mg/kg (four injections) and 25 mg/kg (four injections). Control group of mice received 16 s/c injections of saline. Bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR) to Metacholin (Mch) was measured by pneumography 24 h after the last INA. Results: Anti-G6 IgE AB was elevated in the beginning ASIT reaching maximal level after the 3rd stage of s/c injections (dose 5 mg/kg) and decreased after the 4th stage of s/c injections (dose 25 mg/kg) in compare to non-treated group. Heterogeneity of antibody responses among clinical responders following grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: Biomarkers of clinical efficacy are of major interest to monitor patients under specific sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). To identify such surrogates, we investigated seric and mucosal antibody responses in the context of a randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber. Methods: Changes in titres and affinity of allergen-specific IgE, IgG1-4, IgM and IgA were monitored in serum and nasal secretions in a cohort of 82 grass pollen allergic patients receiving once daily a sublingual 300IR grass pollen tablet or a placebo for 4 months. Average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) was evaluated before and after 1 week, 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment, during allergen challenges in a pollen chamber. Results: A significant clinical response was observed in the group receiving the active treatment. The latter was documented in patients exhibiting distinct patterns of IgE sensitization (i.e. narrow, intermediate, broad) against Phl p 1 to 12 allergens. No neosensitization to grass pollen allergens was observed in the course of SLIT. Responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. Comparing antibody responses from patients belonging to each of the four following groups: Placebo responders/Placebo non responders/Active responders/Active non responders, we could establish that (i) Placebo responders exhibit clear grass pollen-specific antibody responses in nasal mucosa and (ii) Active responders are heterogeneous, encompassing both 'immunoreactive' patients with strong grass pollen-specific IgG, IgE and IgG4 responses (possibly blocking antibodies) induced during SLIT, as well as 'non immunoreactive' responders with no detectable immune responses distinguishing them from patients receiving placebo. Importantly, patients with high symptoms scores at inclusion were all improved under SLIT, although specific IgE levels prior to treatment were not predictive. Conclusion: SLIT with a grass pollen extract is similarly efficacious in patients exhibiting sensitization to single or multiple grass pollen allergens. Responders include both patients with strong seric allergen-specific antibody responses or lacking such responses. The latter observation suggests that additional immune mechanisms distinct from blocking antibodies are involved in SLIT efficacy.
Determination of sulfidoleukotrienes production in patients with atopic dermatitis; Atopic dermatitis (AD) is still the most common skin disorder in children and affects 80-90% of the children younger than 5 years. Also, children with AD have the highest incidence of food allergy. It is now apparent that food hypersensitivity plays a significant pathogenic role in up to 40% of children with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis. A number of investigations have shown the guiding role of inflammation, and particularly of leukotrienes (LT) in allergy development. Sulfido-leukotrienes (sLT) are important mediators in allergic diseases that are synthesized after allergen-specific stimulation. These newly-formed mediators show powerful pro-inflammatory activities inducing oedema, increased vascular permeability, mucous secretion, smooth muscle contraction and chemotaxis of target cells. Cellular antigen stimulation test (CAST) was adapted for the quantitative determination of sulfidoleukotrienes release after in vitro stimulation of leukocytes with specific antigens. In this study, we assessed the diagnostic sensitivity of CAST technique after food and inhalant allergen stimulation in patients with atopic dermatitis. Fifty-three children at the age from 9 months to 14 years with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to inhalant and food allergens were studied. We tested the most frequent allergens connected with AD such as: Der p, Der f, grass pollen, ragweed pollen, birch pollen, cow milk, eggs, soya and wheat. Of all cases, 63% (25/40) of patients had CAST test positive to Der p, 65% (15/23) of patients to Der f, 22% (2/ 9) of patients to grass pollen, 25% (2/8) of patients to ragweed pollen and 29% (2/7) of patients to birch pollen. Our results also show that CAST test was positive in 29% (10/34) of patients with allergy to cow milk, 60% (24/40) of patients to eggs, 50% (5/10) of patients to soya and 38% (6/16) of patients to wheat. Findings in this study suggest that CAST test used for confirmation of allergy status in children with AD is more sensitive to allergens such as Der p, Der f, eggs and soya, than to other tested allergens.

Persistence of specific grass pollen immunotherapies are similar to those observed in other long-term treatment regimens; Background: Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is a valid treatment option for moderateto-severe seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis (SAR) caused by grass pollen. However, there are few data on persistence with long-term SIT regimens. Methods: Individual prescriptions/refill as a proxy for persistence (i.e. defined as the length of time during which the patient continues to be engaged with the prescribed dosing regimen) for three different SIT modalities (subcutaneous immunotherapy immunotherapy (SCIT) with natural allergens, SCIT with modified allergens (allergoids) and sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) with natural pollen extract solutions) were retrospectively tracked over 3 years (2005, 2006 and 2007) in a representative database of patients in Germany (INSIGHT Health). We determined whether SIT-naive patients receiving their first immunotherapy prescription in 2005 had renewed it for the same product group in 2006 and again in 2007. Results: A total of 1410 patients started SIT in 2005 with 112, 695 and 602 for natural extract SLIT, natural extract SCIT and allergoid SCIT, respectively). The distribution of the patients across the three groups reflects the documented market shares for these three SIT modalities in Germany. In 2006, the prescription renewal rates were 71%, 55% and 59%, respectively. In 2007, the rates (relative to 2005) were 51%, 34% and 39%. There were no significant differences between natural extract SCIT and allergoid SCIT (P = 0.1665 in 2006 and P = 0.0605 in 2007, in a chi-squared test) in terms of renewal. Prescription renewal rates for natural extract SLIT were significantly higher than those for natural extract SCIT (P = 0.0015 for 2006 and P = 0.0003 for 2007) and allergoid SCIT (P = 0.0152 for 2006 and P = 0.0111 for 2007). These findings confirm the issue of non-persistence with therapy in other chronic diseases in which non persistence at 6 months after start of therapy is as high as 50%. Conclusion: In a representative, German prescription database, all grass pollen SCIT and SLIT modalities displayed similar long-term prescription renewal rates to those observed in other chronic therapeutic regimens (diabetes, cardiovascular disease and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, for example). Furthermore, our prescription renewal rate data counter the preconceived notion that SCIT (with injection in a medical environment) necessarily results in better overall persistence than SLIT (usually administered at home).
A role for phenology to appraise the really causative species in grass pollinosis; Background: Grass pollen is a worlwide cause of respiratory allergy throughout the world. Patients experience symptoms only when the pollen grains to which they are allergic are in the air and the level of symptoms is generally related to the pollen count. Identifying the causative grass species is essential when allergy is treated with specific immunotherapy (SIT). In fact, the allergen extract for SIT should contain the really responsible botanical species. Methods: We performed a phenological study to assess the flowering of different grass species. The following grasses were sampled: Black grass, Sweet vernal grass, Common wild oat, Barren brome, Cocksfoot, Tall fescue, Yorkshire fog, Perennial ryegrass, Timothy, Bulbous meadow-grass, Kentucky bluegrass (Pooideae), Bermuda grass (Chloridoideae). Ten areas in northern, central, and southern Italy, were chosen, with a total number of 50 stations. The recognition of the phenological flowering phase was performed using an electronmicroscopy based method for the detection of stamens spreading and release of pollen grains. The period of grass pollination was established according to the Italian official pollen calendars. Results: Evident differences were found between grass pollen counts and full flowering of the grass species assessed by phenology, with pollen peaks due only to some species and a relevant pollen load for various species also out of the peak periods. In particular, important Pooideae such as timothy are not present during the pollen peak in the north and centre of Italy and the same occurs with Bermuda grass over the entire territory. Conclusion: The clinical outcome of SIT is strictly dependent on the administration of an allergen extract fitting with patient's IgE sensitization. Concerning grasses, the use of a mixture seems to better reflect the natural exposure of the Italian population, and has the potential to provide a more complete interaction with the immunologic profile of grass sensitized patients.

The clinical development of specific immunotherapies: Specific methodological issues and clinical interpretation of results; Background: Historically, the safety and efficacy of specific immunotherapy (SIT) has been demonstrated in (mainly small-scale) studies and confirmed in meta-analyses. However, the inherent sources of heterogeneity (patient selection outside the pollen season, pollen count variations, long evaluation periods) observed in recent, large-scale studies of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets mean that highly susceptible patients may not exhibit uniformly a sufficient level of symptoms during the study period to assess the efficacy of SIT. Methods: We performed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational clinical trials of a 300IR pre- and co-seasonally administered 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet in adults and children with allergic rhinitis. The primary efficacy criterion was the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) over the pollen season, during which daily grass pollen counts were measured locally. To evaluate the potential relationship between disease severity and the treatment effect, investigating centres were divided in tiertiles according to their mean placebo group ARTSS. Results: Pre-seasonal inclusion of patients on the basis of retrospectively severe symptoms in the previous pollen season did not produce such a severely affected population in the study season. The apparent treatment effect of SLIT tablet was partially masked by the highly variable severity of symptoms during the whole pollen season (mean ARTSS in the adult placebo group: 4.93 ± 3.229). For the adult trial, the mean active versus placebo ARTSSs and the relative difference versus placebo (%) were 15%, 26% and 37% for the low, moderate- and high-disease severity tiertiles, respectively. In the paediatric trial, these values were 10%, 33% and 34%, respectively. Linear regression of individual daily RTSS scores and pollen counts in active and placebo groups also showed that the more severe the disease, the greater the treatment effect of SLIT tablet. Conclusion: Inherent sources of heterogeneity must be taken into account when interpreting the results of natural-exposure immunotherapy trials but none obscured the statistically significant treatment effect of SLIT. In a subgroup analysis, SLIT tablets' beneficial effect increased with disease severity.

Long-lasting clinical efficacy of allergen specific immunotherapy in adults; Background: Many controlled studies have demonstrated that allergen immunotherapy is the unique specific and effective treatment of allergic rhinitis (AR) and/or asthma. The control group composed of patients not receiving SIT during the same period. The two groups were well matched in terms of age, onset of disease and severity, and allergen sensitivity. Patients who had eligible medical records were invited for assessment in 2007 in terms of their symptoms, drug intake, skin test and non-specific bronchial reactivity since the end of the previous SIT in 2000. SIT and control groups were comparatively evaluated regarding at the beginning (T0), end of the SIT (T1) and the current status (T2). Results: Out of 154 patients, 30 SIT (F/M: 21/9, mean age: 30 ± 7.4 years) and 26 control group (F/M: 19/7, mean age: 31.3 ± 7.2 years) provided inclusion criteria. Rhinitis, asthma and medication scores were significantly reduced at T2 compared to T0 and T1 (P = 0.000). Duration of SIT for a longer periods was found to be only independent factor affecting good clinical response. Conclusion: Our study indicates that there is still an important clinical benefit average 7 years after discontinuation of SIT in adults. A striking finding of this study was not prevented development of new sensitization by the SIT. Neverthless, it seems that SIT may play a suppressive role in the onset of overt clinical symptoms.

Tolerability, safety and compliance of rush sublingual immunotherapy with monomeric allergoid tablets; Background: The experience of the last years with SLIT has led to progressively reduce the duration of the up-dosing, starting sometimes already with the maintenance dose. Safety of a rush immunotherapy build-up schedule with depigmented polymerized allergen extracts; Conventional subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) for allergy treatment needs several injections over several weeks to reach the maintenance dose. Shorter up-dosing regimens are desired but limited by the potential of side effects. This study was designed to compare the safety of Depigoid (Laboratorios LETI, Spain) - SCIT 1 day versus 3 weeks up-dosing in patients with Type 1 allergy caused by clinically relevant sensitization against tree pollen, grass pollen, and house-dust mites. A total of 303 patients with confirmed allergic rhinitis/conjunctivitis were included. A rush build-up schedule administering 0.2 mL and then 0.3 mL of the concentrate at day 1 followed by 0.5 mL at day 28 was compared with a conventional 4-week build-up schedule. The number of patients reaching the maintenance phase without systemic reactions or major deviation from treatment schedule were compared. Of the rush 91.8% and in the conventional group 90.9% reached the maintenance phase without dose modification. Neither the proportions of patients with systemic reactions (5.8% rush versus 2% conventional) nor the proportions of patients with local reactions differed significantly between the two regimens (24% rush versus 11% conventional). There was no difference with respect to the applied allergen group. The proposed rush build-up schedule for the immunotherapy treatment with depigmented allergoids without premedication is safe and not inferior to the conventional schedule. ▼Grazax for hay fever - What's new?; In 2008, we reviewed Grazax, a sublingual tablet containing standardised allergen extract of grass pollen.1 At the time, this product was licensed for the treatment of adults with proven grass-pollen-induced rhinitis and conjunctivitis (hay fever). However, we were not convinced that the effect on rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores in published trials was clinically relevant. Also, given that no published studies had compared Grazax with symptomatic therapies or subcutaneous immunotherapy for hay fever, it was expensive and its long-term efficacy and safety were not known, we could not recommend its use.1 Since our review, the terms of the marketing authorisation for Grazax have been changed, such that it is now described in the summary of product characteristics (SPC) as a "disease-modifying treatment", and the drug is now also licensed for use in children aged 5 years and above.2 Here we assess the latest evidence for Grazax and reconsider the drug's place in the management of patients with hay fever.

Allergen immunotherapy in asthma: Current status and future perspectives; Allergen immunotherapy targets Th2 cells activated by specific allergens, which constitutes the basis of allergic disease. Therefore, this approach has therapeutic potential for a variety of allergic diseases, including asthma, and may modify their natural course. Immunotherapy results in systemic immunological changes to allergens, thereby providing clinical benefits in allergic asthma. For example, immunotherapy attenuates T-cell-mediated airway inflammation by down-modulating Th2 and inducing Th1 differentiation. In addition, immunotherapy induces regulatory T cells, which produce IL-10. Meta-analysis has demonstrated that allergen immunotherapy improves clinical symptoms and non-specific airway hyperresponsiveness in asthma, and decreases drug requirements. Clinical studies have supported the usefulness if immunotherapy in mild to moderate asthma cases, particularly in patients with concomitant rhinitis. Several promising novel approaches have emerged as future immunotherapeutic strategies for the treatment of asthma. Current pharmacotherapy, including inhalational corticosteroids, provides powerful anti-symptomatic benefits in asthma

Mimotope vaccination for therapy of allergic asthma: Anti-inflammatory effects in a mouse model; Background: One of the concerns of allergen-specific immunotherapy is the possible boost of inflammatory allergen-specific T lymphocytes. Objective: In this study, we examined the therapeutic potency of a single mimotope, mimicking a structural IgE epitope of grass pollen allergen Phl p 5 in an established memory mouse model of acute allergic asthma. Methods: In the experimental set-up, BALB/c mice were primed with intraperitoneal injections of recombinant Phl p 5a (rPhl p 5a) and subsequently aerosol challenged with the nebulized allergen. Despite not affecting the levels of pre-existing IgE, vaccination with the single mimotope thus rendered anti-inflammatory effects in a mouse model of acute asthma. Conclusion: From our data, we conclude that vaccination with a mimotope peptide representing a single IgE epitope of the allergen Phl p 5a and being devoid of allergen-specific T cell epitopes is able to down-regulate inflammation in acute asthma. © 2009 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.

Does specific immunotherapy act on innate immunity?; Specific immunotherapy (SIT), whether it be subcutaneous or sublingual, relies upon several intricate antigen-specific immune mechanisms, including the modulation of CD4+ T cell responses (stimulation of Th1 and T Reg responses), as well as the induction of anti-inflammatory "blocking" antibodies (IgG4 or IgA). The impact of SIT on innate immunity (i. E., antigen-independent) has yet to be investigated, but may encompass a direct effect on epithelial cells, dendritic cells (DCs), and/or mast cells and basophils. Mucous epithelial cells are the first to come in contact with allergen, and their response to this stimulus differs between allergic and non-allergic individuals. SIT has been reported to modulate the function of plasmacytoid DCs in the peripheral blood (with induction of IFNα secretion following stimulation with a TLR9 ligand), and the question is raised as to whether SIT can elicit a "tolerogenic" phenotype in DCs. With this in view, we are currently engaged in a proteomic study aiming to identify potential molecular markers of regulatory DCs. SIT appears to have an effect on the activation of tissue mast cells and circulating basophils (probably via regulation of activation signals). Nonetheless, our recent SLIT study in grass pollen allergic patients dœs not confirm a correlation between clinical efficacy and a decrease in circulating basophil activation. © 2010 Elsevier Masson SAS. All rights reserved.
